newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Busang shock seen heaviest on smaller mining firms.
newsitem.headline: Busang shock seen heaviest on smaller mining firms.

text.p: Indonesia's Busang gold shock is likely to have the heaviest impact on smaller mining companies who conduct the bulk of exploration around the world, mining executives in Jakarta said on Monday.

Some executives said an interim report released in Canada by consultants Strathcona Mineral Services Ltd that assayed samples showed no commercial gold values in the sector of Busang surveyed was not unexpected.
But they expressed shock at the apparent size of the fraud, which Strathcona said appeared to be "without precedent in the history of mining anywhere in the world".
"It's shocking," one senior executive said.
"It's damaging news for the mining industry in Indonesia," another said.

The Strathcona report was released by the small Canadian mining firm Bre-X Minerals Ltd, which earlier this year had put gold reserves at Busang in East Kalimantan province at over 70 million ounces, making it the find of the century.
Last month Bre-X rocked the mining world and investors by saying the amount of gold might have been overestimated.
Test drills by U.S. giant Freeport McMoRan Copper and Gold Inc in what was meant to be the richest part of the Busang property had found negligible amounts of gold.
Freeport, which had taken a 15 percent stake in Busang and was to develop the property dependent on an exhaustive "due diligence" survey, said it hoped to issue a statement later.
One senior mining source said one impact would be that "the 'juniors' will have a very difficult time funding their programmes."
The juniors are small mining companies responsible for the bulk of exploration and discoveries, which are then exploited by the major companies with the development funds and expertise.
The executive said there was also the danger of a backlash within Indonesia against junior companies.
Bre-X has a 45 percent stake in Busang, and Indonesian interests hold the remaining 40 percent.
Some mining sources believed Indonesia could be acutely embarrassed by the Busang report, particularly with top level involvement after a messy fight for control of the property late last year.
The Nusamba Group chaired by Muhammad "Bob" Hasan, a close friend and adviser of President Suharto, has a 25 percent stake in the property.
Nusamba is 80 percent owned by three charities headed by Suharto, and 10 percent each by Hasan and Suharto's eldest son.
"I expect there will be acute discomfort and repercussions. Certainly there will be much higher prescriptive control, much more bureaucratic intervention," one source said.
Another senior mining executive said he believed however that Busang should not be a major disaster for Indonesia if handled properly.
"If the Indonesian government lets Canada, the Securities Commission and the courts deal with it, it gets taken care of by itself," he said.
Analysts doubted there would be a major effect on Indonesia's attitude towards foreign investment.
"I think they need foreign investment and they're aware of it," one said.
